l1: Fixing an image made by light, without anyone drawing it.
l2: Before photography, every image was filtered through a human hand and a human choice. A photograph is made by the light itself, which gave it an authority no painting had — and which turned out to be partly an illusion, since framing, timing and processing are all choices. Still, it changed evidence, memory, news and identity.
l3: Surviving early plates, patents and process manuals document the chemistry. The first photographs are datable and their processes reproducible; modern practitioners still make daguerreotypes with period methods.
ev: Surviving plates; process patents; reproduction of historic processes
caution: A photograph is not a neutral record. Framing, exposure and processing are all editorial choices, long before digital manipulation existed.

l1: Burning fuel inside the cylinder instead of under a boiler.
l2: Moving combustion inside removes the boiler, the water and most of the mass. The result is far more power per kilogram, which is exactly what a vehicle needs and what a steam engine could not deliver. Every consequence of personal mobility and powered flight follows from that ratio.
l3: Otto's four-stroke cycle of 1876 is documented in patents and surviving engines. Thermodynamic analysis explains the efficiency ceiling, and it matches measured performance.
ev: Otto-cycle patents; surviving engines; thermodynamic analysis

l1: Personal transport that goes where there is no track and no timetable.
l2: The car offers door-to-door travel on individual schedule, and people have consistently valued that enough to accept its costs. Those costs are substantial and were mostly unforeseen: cities rebuilt around parking and roads, a large annual toll of deaths, and a major share of global emissions.
l3: Production and registration statistics, road-network data, and casualty and emissions series document both the adoption and its consequences over more than a century.
ev: Production and registration statistics; casualty and emissions data
caution: Mass motorisation reshaped cities and carries large ongoing costs in casualties and emissions. Convenience and cost belong in the same account.

l1: Heavier-than-air machines that stay up on purpose.
l2: The Wrights' decisive contribution was not lift — that was understood — but control. They solved three-axis control, which is what turns a glider into an aircraft you can fly deliberately. They also built a wind tunnel and generated their own aerodynamic data because the published tables were wrong.
l3: The Wright Flyer is held by the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. The brothers' notebooks, wind-tunnel data, patents and photographs of the 1903 flights survive and are well studied.
ev: Wright Flyer; notebooks and wind-tunnel data; 1903 photographs

l1: Still images shown fast enough that the eye reads motion.
l2: Cinema exploits a limitation of human perception and builds an art form on it. More than that, it invented a grammar — cut, close-up, cross-cut, montage — for assembling time so that an audience constructs a story from fragments. Every screen medium since, video games included, inherited that vocabulary.
l3: Surviving films, projection equipment, patents and studio records document the technology and its language. Early films are dated and their techniques directly analysable frame by frame.
ev: Surviving films and equipment; patents; studio records

l1: A glass bulb that controls electrons — the first electronic component.
l2: The vacuum tube can amplify a weak signal and switch on and off with no moving parts, which is exactly what radio, long-distance telephony and early computers required. It was also hot, fragile, power-hungry and prone to failure — the ENIAC's tubes failed often enough that finding the dead one was a routine task.
l3: Surviving tubes and equipment, patents, and the maintenance logs of early computers document both capability and failure rate. The Computer History Museum holds machines and components.
ev: Surviving tubes and machines; patents; maintenance logs

l1: Using small currents to control other currents.
l2: Electrical engineering moves power; electronics moves information. Once a device can amplify and switch, signals can be processed rather than merely transmitted — and switching is what makes logic physically possible. Every computer is, at bottom, a very large arrangement of switches.
l3: Component development, circuit theory and the standards that made mass-produced electronics possible are documented in patents, engineering literature and IEEE milestone records.
ev: Patents; circuit theory literature; engineering standards

l1: Communication with no wire between the ends.
l2: Radio removes the last physical constraint on communication. It reaches ships at sea, aircraft, remote regions and — crucially — everyone at once, which made mass broadcasting possible and gave the twentieth century its characteristic political instrument. Every wireless technology since is a descendant.
l3: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves; Hertz demonstrated them; Marconi and others engineered practical transmission. Patents, the maritime distress record and broadcasting archives document the development.
ev: Hertz's experiments; patents; maritime and broadcast records

l1: A material that conducts electricity only when you tell it to.
l2: Semiconductors sit between conductor and insulator, and adding controlled trace impurities — doping — tunes exactly how they behave. That controllability is the whole basis of modern electronics: it lets a switch be built with no moving parts, at a scale limited only by how precisely the material can be patterned.
l3: Semiconductor physics is documented in the research literature and in the Nobel citation for the transistor. Purity and doping requirements are recorded in process specifications; the achieved purity of silicon is among the highest of any bulk material made.
ev: Semiconductor physics literature; process specifications

l1: A switch with no moving parts, and it can be made almost arbitrarily small.
l2: The transistor does what the vacuum tube did, using a fraction of the power, in a fraction of the space, with far greater reliability. Crucially, it gets better as it gets smaller — which is the property that made decades of exponential improvement possible. It is arguably the most-manufactured object in human history.
l3: The 1947 Bell Labs work by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley was recognised with the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect'. Laboratory notebooks and the original devices survive.
ev: Bell Labs notebooks; original devices; Nobel Prize record

l1: Many components made together on one piece of material, wired in place.
l2: The problem the IC solved was not size but connections — a circuit with thousands of separately soldered parts is unbuildable and unreliable. Fabricating components and their wiring simultaneously on one substrate removes the assembly step entirely, and the cost per component then falls as the count rises. That inversion is what makes cheap computing possible.
l3: Kilby's and Noyce's devices, patents and fabrication records are held and documented by the Computer History Museum. Transistor-count series over decades quantify the scaling directly.
ev: Original devices and patents; transistor-count series

l1: A machine that follows a stored list of instructions, whatever they say.
l2: Earlier machines did one thing. The decisive idea — a machine holding its instructions in the same memory as its data — makes one machine capable of any computable task, including modifying its own program. Generality is the whole point: the hardware stops determining the application.
l3: Early machines and their documentation survive: Colossus, ENIAC, the Manchester Baby, EDSAC. Turing's 1936 paper set out the theoretical model before the machines existed, and it still describes what they can and cannot do.
ev: Surviving early machines; design reports; Turing's 1936 paper
caution: There is no single inventor of the computer. Several machines in Britain, the United States and Germany have competing claims depending on which criteria are used.

l1: Writing the instructions the machine will follow.
l2: Programming is where computing stops being electrical engineering and becomes something closer to writing. Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, published in 1843, argued that such a machine could operate on symbols generally rather than only on numbers — the idea that the machine is not merely a calculator.
l3: Lovelace's published notes survive, as do early program listings, punched cards and machine documentation. Programming's history includes the substantial and long-underacknowledged contribution of women, documented in institutional records.
ev: Lovelace's 1843 notes; early program listings; punched cards

l1: Fast storage the processor can reach immediately.
l2: A computer's speed is limited as much by how fast it can reach data as by how fast it can calculate. That gap has widened for decades, which is why modern machines are built as layered hierarchies of caches. Much of the art of fast software is really the art of arranging data so the memory system cooperates.
l3: Magnetic core memory planes, delay lines and later semiconductor memory survive in museum collections, alongside the engineering documentation and access-time specifications that make the hierarchy visible.
ev: Surviving memory hardware; access-time specifications

l1: Keeping data when the power goes off.
l2: Persistent storage is what lets computers accumulate rather than merely calculate. Cost per byte has fallen by something like eight orders of magnitude since the 1950s, and that decline — more than processor speed — is what made it reasonable to keep everything instead of deciding what to discard.
l3: IBM's RAMAC of 1956, the first hard disk drive, is documented and preserved. Long-run cost-per-byte series quantify the decline across tape, disk and solid-state generations.
ev: RAMAC and successor drives; cost-per-byte series

date: ≈ 1950s CE onward as a distinct thing
l1: The part of the machine that has no physical existence.
l2: Software separated from hardware and became an industry, an art and a permanent maintenance problem. Its distinguishing economics: essentially zero cost to copy, very high cost to build correctly, and a defect rate that no amount of care eliminates. Most large software failures are failures of complexity management, not of coding.
l3: Source code, version histories, defect databases and post-mortem reports of major failures are extensively documented. Historic source is preserved by museums and archives, including operating systems and language compilers.
ev: Preserved source code; version histories; failure post-mortems

l1: A whole processor on a single chip.
l2: Putting the processor on one inexpensive component turned computing from an institutional asset into a part you could design into anything — a till, a car, a washing machine, a watch, a phone. Far more microprocessors are sold into embedded uses than into anything recognisable as a computer.
l3: The Intel 4004 of 1971 and its successors are preserved and documented, with die photographs, datasheets and production figures. Transistor-count and price series track the trajectory.
ev: Preserved chips and datasheets; die photographs; production figures

l1: A computer owned by a person rather than an institution.
l2: The shift is about control as much as cost. When the machine belongs to you, you decide what it runs, and a hobbyist can write and distribute software without asking anyone. That is the precondition for most of the software culture, and most of the games, that followed.
l3: Machines, manuals, user-group newsletters and software libraries from the period are preserved. Sales figures and household penetration statistics document adoption.
ev: Preserved machines and software; user-group publications; sales data

l1: Making pictures by calculating them.
l2: Graphics made computers usable by people who are not programmers. Sutherland's Sketchpad in 1963 demonstrated direct manipulation — draw on the screen, the machine responds — and that idea leads to every graphical interface since. It also means images can be generated from a model rather than captured from the world.
l3: Sketchpad is documented in Sutherland's thesis and in film of the system running. The Computer History Museum's graphics and games timeline records the subsequent development in detail.
ev: Sketchpad thesis and film; museum timeline; early systems

l1: Sound, image and text reduced to numbers.
l2: Once media is numbers, copying is exact and free, editing is non-destructive, and transmission is just data. Every business model built on the scarcity of physical copies broke, and the resulting fights over copyright, distribution and value are still running four decades later.
l3: Format specifications, compression standards and the recorded history of the industries affected — music, film, publishing — document the transition, alongside revenue and distribution statistics.
ev: Format and compression standards; industry revenue series

l1: Machines that can talk to each other.
l2: Connecting computers changes what a computer is for. Alone it computes; connected it communicates, and the communication turns out to matter more. Packet switching — chopping messages into pieces routed independently — was the key idea, and it is what makes a network survive damage and share capacity efficiently.
l3: ARPANET's design documents, the Requests for Comments series and the original hardware are preserved. The RFC archive is a continuous public record of how the protocols were argued out.
ev: ARPANET documentation; RFC series; preserved hardware

l1: A network of networks that no one owns or controls.
l2: The internet's design choice was to keep the network simple and push intelligence to the edges. That is why it could be extended by anyone without permission — the network does not need to know what your application does. Nearly everything unexpected that happened on it is a consequence of that decision.
l3: The design rationale is documented by its architects in 'A Brief History of the Internet', and the entire protocol development is public in the RFC series. Growth is tracked by host counts and adoption statistics.
ev: Architects' published history; RFC series; adoption statistics

l1: Documents that link to each other across the whole network.
l2: The web is an application running on the internet, not the internet itself — a distinction worth keeping. Its contribution was making the network usable by people rather than by systems administrators: a naming scheme, a markup language and a protocol, given away rather than licensed.
l3: Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal at CERN survives, as do the first server and browser. CERN has reconstructed the original browser, and the early specifications are public.
ev: 1989 CERN proposal; first server and browser; specifications

l1: The program through which most people experience the network.
l2: The browser started as a document viewer and became the most widely used application platform on Earth. Adding images, then scripting, then graphics and audio turned a page reader into a runtime — which is why so much software now ships as a website rather than as a program you install.
l3: Early browsers are preserved and runnable, and the standards that define browser behaviour are public. Market share and capability timelines document the platform's expansion.
ev: Preserved browsers; public web standards; market share data

l1: Talking to anyone, anywhere, essentially free.
l2: The cost of sending a message fell effectively to zero, and volume rose accordingly. The consequences cut both ways: contact maintained across any distance, and also attention markets, information cascades and harassment at scale. The technology is the same in both cases; the difference is in the incentives layered on top.
l3: Message-volume statistics, platform adoption data and a large research literature on social effects document the change. Early email and messaging systems are preserved.
ev: Traffic and adoption statistics; preserved early systems
caution: Effects on attention, polarisation and wellbeing are actively researched and contested. Strong claims in either direction outrun the evidence.

l1: A networked computer that is always with you.
l2: The smartphone folds together the computer, the camera, the map, the telephone, the music player and the payment card, and the important part is that it is always on and always connected. For a majority of people alive today it is the primary computer, and for many it was the first.
l3: Shipment and penetration statistics, teardown analyses of components, and connectivity data document adoption. Our World in Data tracks mobile subscription and internet access rates globally.
ev: Shipment and penetration statistics; component teardowns

l1: Someone else's computers, rented by the minute.
l2: The cloud turns capital expenditure into operating expenditure, which lets a small team command computing capacity that once required a corporation. That is genuinely democratising and it is also concentrating: a handful of providers now host a large share of the world's services, and their outages are everyone's outages.
l3: Provider capacity disclosures, energy consumption reporting for data centres, and market concentration figures document scale. Outage post-mortems are public and show dependency structure.
ev: Provider disclosures; data-centre energy reporting; outage records

l1: Systems that perform tasks previously thought to require a mind.
l2: The field's history is a cycle of overpromise and retrenchment. What changed in the 2010s was not a conceptual breakthrough so much as scale: much more data, much more compute, and learned representations replacing hand-written rules. What these systems actually understand — if that word applies — remains genuinely unsettled.
l3: Training-compute series, benchmark results and published model papers document capability growth. Our World in Data tracks compute used in notable AI systems over decades, showing an extremely steep curve.
ev: Training-compute series; benchmark results; published research
caution: Claims about machine understanding, reasoning and consciousness are contested and often overstated in both directions. Benchmark performance is not the same as competence.

date: Games are ancient; the discipline is recent
l1: Designing rules that make voluntary difficulty enjoyable.
l2: Games long predate computers — the Royal Game of Ur is roughly 4,500 years old and its rules have been partially reconstructed from a cuneiform tablet. What game design adds is deliberate authorship of a system whose whole purpose is to be interesting to inhabit: rules, feedback, difficulty curve, and meaningful choice.
l3: Ancient board games survive with boards, pieces and, occasionally, written rules. Modern design is documented in design documents, playtest records and postmortems published by developers.
ev: Ancient board games and rule tablets; design documents; playtest records

l1: A computed world that responds to what you do.
l2: Every earlier medium presents; a game responds. That difference makes the audience a participant whose choices change what happens, which is why games can teach systems in a way film and text cannot — you learn a rule by living inside it rather than being told it.
l3: Spacewar!, written in 1962 on a PDP-1, is preserved and still runs on restored hardware at the Computer History Museum. Earlier experiments such as Tennis for Two are documented, and priority claims are argued in the literature.
ev: Spacewar! on restored PDP-1; preserved systems; industry records

l1: A computer built for one purpose, sold at a price that assumes you will buy games.
l2: Fixed hardware is a gift to developers: every unit is identical, so a game can be optimised to the exact machine in a way PC software never can. That is why consoles historically punched above their raw specifications, and why late-generation games look so much better than launch titles on identical hardware.
l3: Consoles, development kits and technical documentation are preserved. Sales figures and the recorded history of the 1983 market crash document the industry's volatility.
ev: Preserved consoles and dev kits; technical documentation; sales data

l1: Building a model in three dimensions and computing the view.
l2: A 3D scene stores geometry, not pictures — so the camera can be anywhere, and the image is produced on demand. That is what makes a navigable space possible rather than a set of prepared views, and it is the technical precondition for every open world in this graph.
l3: Foundational algorithms — hidden surface removal, Gouraud and Phong shading, texture mapping, Z-buffering — are documented in published papers, most from the University of Utah group in the 1970s, and are still in use.
ev: Published rendering algorithms; early systems; museum collections

l1: Drawing a complete image in about sixteen milliseconds, sixty times a second.
l2: Real-time rendering is engineering under a hard deadline. A film frame can take hours; a game frame cannot take longer than the budget, ever, or the illusion breaks. Almost every technique in real-time graphics is an approximation chosen because it looks close enough and finishes in time.
l3: GPU architectures, graphics APIs and the published research on real-time approximation techniques document the field. Frame-time profiling makes the budget directly measurable.
ev: GPU architecture documentation; graphics APIs; published techniques

l1: Software that makes objects fall, collide and topple plausibly.
l2: A physics engine is not physics. It is a set of approximations tuned to look right and run fast, and it will happily violate conservation laws if that produces a better result. This is a useful thing to know about simulation generally: fidelity is chosen against cost, and 'realistic' usually means 'convincing'.
l3: Engine source, technical papers on collision detection and constraint solvers, and developer documentation describe the methods and their known failure modes explicitly.
ev: Engine source and documentation; published simulation methods
caution: Game physics is deliberately inaccurate. It optimises for plausibility and speed, not for correctness.

l1: Motion authored frame by frame, or generated between keys.
l2: Animation is the study of how movement communicates. The principles worked out by hand animators — anticipation, follow-through, timing, weight — transferred directly to computer animation, because they describe perception rather than technique. A character reads as alive because of timing, not polygon count.
l3: Animation principles are documented in the practitioner literature and remain standard teaching. Digital animation techniques — skeletal rigging, blending, inverse kinematics — are described in published research and tool documentation.
ev: Practitioner literature; published animation research; production records

l1: Recording a real performance and driving a digital character with it.
l2: Motion capture solves the problem that human observers are extremely good at spotting wrong human movement. Recording an actual performer gets the micro-timing right in a way hand animation struggles to. It also relocates authorship: the performance is the actor's, and the industry took a while to acknowledge that.
l3: Capture systems, calibration methods and production pipelines are documented technically. Its ancestor, rotoscoping — tracing filmed footage — dates to the 1910s and is documented in patents.
ev: Capture system documentation; production pipelines; rotoscope patents

l1: Reusable machinery so each game does not rebuild everything from nothing.
l2: Separating engine from content is the industrial move that made large games feasible. It also changed who can make games: engines that are free to start with put a professional toolchain in the hands of individuals, which is why so much of the interesting work now comes from very small teams.
l3: Engine architecture is documented in technical literature and in released source for several historically important engines. Licensing records and credits track adoption across the industry.
ev: Released engine source; architecture literature; licensing records

l1: Content generated by rules instead of placed by hand.
l2: Procedural generation trades authored detail for scale: a rule that makes plausible terrain can fill a continent that no team could build by hand. The permanent tension is that generated content is abundant and rarely memorable, so the strongest uses combine generated bulk with hand-authored landmarks.
l3: Techniques such as Perlin noise, L-systems and wave function collapse are published with implementations. Early examples — Elite fitting a galaxy into a few kilobytes by generating it from a seed — are preserved and analysed.
ev: Published algorithms; preserved early titles; technical postmortems

l1: An urban space you can move through that does not exist.
l2: A convincing virtual city needs more than geometry: traffic that flows, pedestrians with somewhere to be, lighting that changes, sound that comes from the right place. It is a simulation of urban life at just enough depth to survive being looked at, and the interesting engineering is deciding what can be faked.
l3: Development postmortems, technical talks and published research on crowd and traffic simulation document the methods. Real-world reference material — photography, survey data and increasingly lidar — is used in production.
ev: Developer technical talks; crowd and traffic simulation research

l1: A space you can go anywhere in, in any order.
l2: Open-world design gives up control of sequence, which means the designer can no longer guarantee what the player has seen. Everything must work from any direction, at any point, and the story must survive being encountered out of order. That constraint drives an enormous amount of technical and narrative machinery.
l3: Streaming architectures, level-of-detail systems and world-partitioning techniques are documented in engine documentation and developer conference talks.
ev: Engine documentation; developer conference talks; postmortems

l1: Images computed by simulating how light actually behaves.
l2: Physically based rendering models light transport — energy conservation, real material response, actual light paths — rather than approximating an appearance. Doing that within a real-time frame budget required dedicated hardware, and the gap between offline film rendering and real-time rendering has narrowed dramatically as a result.
l3: The rendering equation was formulated in published research in 1986, and path-tracing and physically based material models are extensively documented. Hardware ray-tracing capability is documented in GPU specifications.
ev: Rendering equation literature; PBR material research; GPU specifications

l1: Modelling a system too complex to solve with an equation.
l2: Simulation is a third mode of investigation alongside theory and experiment: when a system cannot be solved analytically and cannot be experimented on, you can compute its behaviour step by step. Climate, galaxies, protein folding and epidemics are all studied this way — as are game worlds, at far lower fidelity.
l3: Monte Carlo methods date to 1940s computing work and are documented in the research literature. Scientific simulation codes and their validation studies are published, and validation against observation is the standard check.
ev: Monte Carlo literature; published simulation codes; validation studies
caution: A simulation is only as good as its assumptions. Agreement with reality must be demonstrated, never assumed.

l1: Characters with routines, goals and reactions of their own.
l2: Game AI is optimised for being interesting rather than for being intelligent. A character that plays optimally is usually no fun, so systems are designed to be readable — the player must be able to infer what the character is doing and why. Much game AI is deliberately handicapped for exactly this reason.
l3: Behaviour trees, goal-oriented action planning and utility systems are documented in technical talks and published game AI literature, including candid accounts of where the illusion breaks.
ev: Game AI literature; developer technical talks; behaviour system documentation
caution: Game AI is generally not machine learning, and it is designed to be beatable. Legibility beats optimality.

l1: Games that borrow the language of film without stopping being games.
l2: There is a real tension here. Cinema controls what you see; games hand that control to the player. Cinematic games negotiate between the two, and the long-running argument about cutscenes is a genuine design disagreement about whether authored moments are worth the cost of taking the controller away.
l3: Production documentation, virtual cinematography techniques and developer talks describe the methods. Comparative analyses of authored versus emergent moments are a standing topic in game criticism.
ev: Production documentation; virtual cinematography research; developer talks

l1: Hundreds of specialists, several years, and budgets comparable to films.
l2: A large modern game is an industrial production: artists, engineers, designers, writers, actors, audio teams, QA, localisation and production management, coordinated across studios and time zones. The scale brings capability and also risk — budgets that require enormous sales, and a well-documented pattern of excessive overtime.
l3: Credits lists, published budget figures, studio headcounts and industry labour reporting document both the scale and the working conditions, including sustained reporting on crunch.
ev: Game credits and headcounts; published budgets; labour reporting
caution: Extended crunch is a documented and recurring feature of large game production, with real costs to the people involved.

l1: A world that keeps running whether or not you are looking at it.
l2: The hard part is not size but persistence: state that survives, systems that continue off-screen, consequences that outlast the moment. Doing it fully is computationally impossible, so every open world is an elaborate arrangement of things that only exist while observed — an engineering trick that the player must never notice.
l3: Streaming, level-of-detail and simulation-culling architectures are documented in engine documentation and developer talks, which describe explicitly what is suspended when nobody is watching.
ev: Engine architecture documentation; developer technical talks

l1: Coordinating thousands of people across years and continents.
l2: At this scale the bottleneck stops being any technology and becomes coordination itself: asset pipelines, version control across terabytes, build systems, review processes, and the organisational design to keep several hundred people from blocking each other. It is much closer to shipbuilding than to writing software alone.
l3: Studio structures, pipeline tooling and production methods are documented in developer talks and postmortems. Employment figures and industry revenue data give the scale.
ev: Studio pipeline documentation; postmortems; industry employment data

l1: A series that made the open city the point rather than the setting.
l2: The series' contribution was treating the environment as the main attraction — a city dense and reactive enough to be worth existing in without a task. That reframing pushed the whole industry toward systemic worlds, and it came with sustained public controversy about content that is part of the record rather than a footnote to it.
l3: Release history, technical postmortems, sales figures and the documented regulatory and public reaction across multiple countries constitute the record.
ev: Release and sales records; technical postmortems; regulatory record
caution: The series has been the subject of long-running debate over violent content. Research on media effects is contested and does not support simple causal claims in either direction.

l1: An unreleased game, standing here for whatever the current edge happens to be.
l2: Pick any endpoint you like — this one is a placeholder for the frontier. What matters is the shape of the thing behind it: a modern game of this kind depends on semiconductor fabrication, real-time rendering research, animation principles from hand-drawn film, physics approximation, network infrastructure, thousands of people and roughly three million years of accumulated technique. No single invention is doing the work.
l3: Rockstar Games announced on its official newswire that the release moved to 19 November 2026, after an earlier date of 26 May 2026, and Take-Two reiterated the 19 November date in its fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on 7 August 2026. As of the last check of this database — 11 September 2026 — the game is unreleased, so nothing here is a claim about the finished product.
ev: Publisher and company announcements (primary sources)
caution: Unreleased at the time of writing. Release dates have moved more than once; treat any schedule as provisional.

l1: A persistent place, shared with other people, that exists only as computation.
l2: When a simulated space is persistent and shared, things start happening in it that nobody designed: economies, governance disputes, property, status, conflict, and real relationships. Virtual worlds have repeatedly become laboratories for social questions, generally by accident and usually to their operators' surprise.
l3: Long-running virtual worlds have been studied by economists, sociologists and legal scholars, with published work on in-world economies, governance and the disease-spread event in one game that epidemiologists analysed as a behavioural model.
ev: Academic studies of virtual economies and governance; platform data
